ANZ pulls first RBA rate cut forward to June 2027, sees three cuts by early 2028
body: The bigger story for currency markets is the policy divergence. The RBA is now widely expected to start easing in mid-2027, while the Fed is still on a hiking path, with a December increase broadly expected. A narrowing rate gap between the two would weigh on the Australian dollar against the US dollar over time. Short-dated Australian rates may see limited reaction, because markets had already priced a June cut as more likely than not after the jobs data. The effect is more likely to show up further out on the curve. Any upside surprise in quarterly inflation would test ANZ's call quickly and could prompt a sharp repricing back toward a later start to easing.
--- After five hikes this year, ANZ thinks the RBA will reverse course by mid-2027, though that depends on inflation cooling faster than the central bank itself expects.

ANZ now expects the Reserve Bank of Australia to begin cutting interest rates in June 2027, five months earlier than its previous forecast of November 2027, making it the first of Australia's big four banks to pencil in relief before the second half of next year.

In a research note released on Tuesday, ANZ Head of Australian Economics Adam Boyton set out a new easing path. The bank now sees a 25 basis point cut in June 2027, taking the cash rate from 4.85% to 4.60%, followed by a second cut in August 2027 to 4.35% and a third in February 2028 to 4.10%. Under its previous forecast, ANZ expected only two cuts, in November 2027 and February 2028.

The change comes less than a month after the RBA delivered its fifth rate increase of 2026 on November 3, lifting the cash rate to 4.85%, its highest level since 2008. The other three major banks currently expect the first cut in August 2027.

Boyton said three conditions need to play out over the next six months to justify a cut in the first half of next year: further deterioration in the labour market, an unwinding of excess demand across the economy and a moderation in underlying inflation. He said there is already early evidence pointing toward each of those developments.

The labour market is the most visible of the three. Employment fell sharply for a second straight month in October, pushing the unemployment rate up to 4.9%, a five-year high. That is above 4.75%, the RBA's estimate of the jobless rate consistent with stable inflation, a threshold that matters because it suggests the jobs market is no longer adding to price pressure.

Inflation is the harder test. The RBA's own forecasts, released after its November meeting, show inflation staying above 3% over the coming year and not returning to the top of its 2% to 3% target band until late 2027. For a June cut to happen, underlying price growth would need to slow faster than the central bank currently expects, or the RBA would need to be convinced that a weakening economy will finish the job.

ANZ's call also brings it closer to market pricing rather than ahead of it. After last week's jobs data, markets put the odds of a quarter-point cut at the June 2027 meeting at around 68%, rising to about 90% for August. Because the forecast still implies an extended hold from here, its main effect is on pricing further out along the yield curve rather than on expectations for the next few RBA meetings.

The key risks to the view run in both directions. A rebound in hiring or stubborn services inflation could push cuts back toward the second half of 2027, while a sharper slowdown could bring them forward again. Quarterly inflation and monthly jobs data over the next six months will decide which way the call breaks.

news.title: Goldman sees up to $15 trillion for AI infrastructure as spending spreads beyond Nvidia
body: Goldman's framing favours the bottleneck parts of the AI supply chain, particularly memory makers, advanced packaging specialists and power infrastructure, over a single-stock bet on Nvidia. That is relevant for Asian equities, where memory and packaging exposure is concentrated in Korea and Taiwan. The view that neocloud lending now depends on milestones should ease some credit concerns around the sector, although it also implies slower, more conditional build-outs. The power angle ties AI spending to energy and utilities demand, a theme that is likely to keep electricity infrastructure in focus as data centre construction grows.
Goldman's message is that the AI build-out is bigger than any one company: even if Nvidia's share shrinks, the trillions keep flowing, just into more hands.

Goldman Sachs believes $10 trillion to $15 trillion could flow into AI infrastructure over the next six years, and argues that a growing share of that spending is reaching companies beyond Nvidia, including memory makers, chip packaging specialists and power suppliers.

The bank's note was written before Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, when the company's leadership was still in doubt. That timing matters. Several of the risks it weighed, including uncertainty over Nvidia's product roadmap, have eased with Huang's return. Its central argument does not depend on who runs Nvidia, though: in Goldman's view, near-term demand for AI infrastructure remains intact.

On the supply side, Goldman said demand is outstripping supply across memory, server processors and chipmaking equipment. Nvidia sells far more than graphics processors, including networking gear, central processors, complete server systems and the software that ties them together. Even so, the bank noted that investment is increasingly reaching areas Nvidia does not supply, such as memory, advanced packaging, which covers how chips are assembled and connected, and power.

That leads to what may be the note's most useful framing for investors. Goldman said any loss of Nvidia market share would change who gets which slice of the AI pie, not the size of the pie. Supply constraints and long design cycles limit how quickly share can shift, but uncertainty over Nvidia's longer-term roadmap could help rival chip designers and their suppliers. The bank also flagged that if Nvidia's work on open-source models and enterprise tools slowed, closed-model developers could benefit at the expense of software firms that rely on fast open-source progress. Huang's return makes that scenario less likely in the near term.

Monday's market reaction offered a live test of the thesis. When Huang returned, memory makers and other AI suppliers rallied alongside Nvidia, consistent with Goldman's view that the AI spending wave lifts a broad supply chain rather than a single company.

For investors, the takeaway is less about Nvidia's leadership drama than about where AI capital is heading next. If Goldman is right that spending is broadening into memory, packaging and power, the bottlenecks in those areas may matter as much for returns as Nvidia's market share. The main risk to that view is a slowdown in AI investment itself, which would shrink the pie rather than reshuffle it.

news.title: Fed's Williams pins inflation on unusual factors, sees 2027 bringing it lower
body: The Q&A softens the tone of Williams' prepared remarks without changing their core message, so pricing for a quarter-point hike on December 9 is unlikely to move much. His focus on unusual factors puts energy back at the centre. Brent is still around $92, well above the roughly $72 seen in late February before the US war with Iran began, so oil remains the main factor in how quickly 2027 delivers the lower inflation he expects. A sustained fall in crude would strengthen the case for a shallower hiking path next year, while fresh supply disruption would push the other way. His caution on hiring matters for the US dollar, since any slowdown in payrolls would weaken the case for further increases beyond December.
Williams still wants inflation lower, but his Q&A made clear he sees shocks rather than an overheating economy behind it, which points to steady hikes rather than aggressive ones.

New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said on Monday that the recent rise in US inflation has been driven by unusual factors and that he expects 2027 to be a year of lower inflation, striking a more measured tone in a question-and-answer session after his prepared remarks.

Speaking at an event at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York City, Williams said the Fed has been working very hard to bring inflation down and had made progress. That did not mark a retreat from his speech, in which he said inflation remains too high, the risks are skewed to the upside and the central bank still has work to do to get back to its 2% goal. His forecasts fit his comment on 2027: he sees inflation ending this year at 3.5%, slowing to just above 2% next year and reaching the target in 2028.

The "unusual factors" line links to the drivers he set out in his prepared text. There he pointed to elevated energy prices, along with tariffs, geopolitical conflicts and the AI investment surge pushing up prices in certain categories of goods, while finding little evidence of those pressures spreading into broader, more persistent inflation. Read together, his remarks suggest he sees the current overshoot as the product of specific shocks rather than an overheating economy. Policymakers who hold that view typically favour a gradual approach to tightening over an aggressive one.

On the economy, Williams said growth has been resilient in the face of many large challenges, though he cautioned that the underpinnings of that strength face some challenges of their own. He also said companies want to hire but are being cautious. That adds a note of caution to his speech, which described the job market as stable and forecast the unemployment rate easing from 4.1% to around 4% next year, alongside growth of 2.75% in both 2026 and 2027.
Williams also stressed that the Fed keeps politics out of its policy debates.

Markets broadly expect the Fed to raise its policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point at its December 8-9 meeting from the current 3.75% to 4.00% range, with further increases expected next year. The Fed last raised rates in September. With that meeting about two weeks away, Williams' comments describe a policymaker still committed to bringing inflation down but alert to softer spots in growth and hiring. That leaves incoming data, and energy prices in particular, to decide how far the Fed goes beyond December.

news.title: Williams keeps December Fed hike in play as inflation seen above 2% until 2028
body: Williams' remarks support pricing for a quarter-point hike in December and further tightening in 2027, which should keep front-end Treasury yields firm and give the US dollar some support. Energy features in his inflation story, and he calls the energy outlook uncertain, so any renewed rise in oil would add to the hawkish case. For equities, his message suggests the Fed will not step back from tightening just because stocks have been volatile, though the AI-led rally shows risk appetite can hold up under a hiking path. If December data come in hot, traders may start pricing a faster pace of increases next year.
Williams sees growth as strong and the labour market as steady, and with inflation not back at target until 2028, he has no reason to take the Fed off its tightening path.

New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said on Monday that inflation remains too high and the US central bank still has work to do to bring it back to its 2% goal, leaving the door open to another rate increase when policymakers meet on December 8 and 9.

In remarks prepared for an event at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York City, Williams said the Fed needs to act over time to return inflation to target in a timely way and keep it there. He added that he will keep weighing incoming data before deciding what the Fed should do at the December meeting, stopping short of committing to a move.

His forecasts underline how long the job could take. Williams expects inflation to finish 2026 at 3.5%, slow to just above 2% next year and reach the target only in 2028. He described the risks to that path as tilted to the upside, pointing to energy prices as one of the main drivers of price pressure and saying their outlook is uncertain.

Williams did offer some reassurance on the breadth of the problem. In his view, tariffs, geopolitical conflicts and the surge in artificial intelligence investment are lifting prices in certain categories of goods, but there is little sign these effects are feeding through into wider, more persistent inflation. He also said the impact of AI on the economy overall remains uncertain.

On growth and jobs, his assessment was upbeat. Williams sees the economy as strong and resilient, forecasting growth of 2.75% in both 2026 and 2027, and described the labour market as stable. He expects the unemployment rate, currently 4.1%, to edge down to around 4% next year.

Markets broadly expect the Fed to lift its policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point in December from the current 3.75% to 4.00% range, with further increases anticipated next year. The Fed last raised rates in September, and inflation has now run above target for more than five years, raising concern among officials that the public could lose faith in a return to 2%.

The remarks landed on a day of sharp gains for stocks, after Nvidia said it was reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive following a push from President Donald Trump. The rally highlighted how heavily markets lean on AI companies, and came after some observers had questioned whether recent equity losses might make the Fed hesitate. Williams' message suggests stock market swings are unlikely to knock the Fed off its focus on inflation.

news.title: Silver sets the technical boundaries in the short term for traders
body: Silver is trading higher today after falling to its lowest level since September 2025 on Friday. The rebound took the price from $40.75 to a session high of $44.25, a gain of about 8.6% from Friday’s low. The move ran into sellers at the 100-hour moving average, however, and the price has since rotated lower.

The broader trend has been lower since September. Silver stalled at $67.30 on September 26 and moved back below its 100-day moving average, which was at $66.59 at the time. From there, the price stepped lower. The November 10 swing high at $53.72 marked the start of the latest leg down, which took silver to $40.75 on Friday.

Friday’s low tested the downward-sloping trendline drawn through the October 14 and October 30 lows. Sellers could not extend the move below that line, giving buyers a level to lean against. A break below the line would have given those buyers a reason to get out quickly. With support holding, silver had room to rebound as gold moved higher and broader risk sentiment improved.

At today’s high near $44.25, silver tested its 100-hour moving average and turned lower. That gives sellers a level to lean against as well. As long as the price stays below that moving average, the rebound remains corrective within the broader downtrend. A move above it that can hold would give buyers their first sign that the short-term bias is shifting in their favor.

On the downside, the falling trendline remains the first support to watch, with Friday’s $40.75 low the nearby reference point. A sustained break below both would put sellers back in control and extend the move to fresh lows.
For now, the buyers defended support and the sellers defended resistance. The next clue will come from which side can break its level and keep the price there.

news.title: Gold rebounds 3.2% despite a stronger dollar and higher yields.
body: Gold is up 3.2% today, trading near $3,654 after falling more than 9% last week and hitting its lowest level since September 2025. The rebound stands out with both the US dollar and Treasury yields moving higher. A stronger dollar makes gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies, while higher yields raise the opportunity cost of holding an asset that pays no interest. So why is gold higher anyway?

The stock market rebound may be helping indirectly. As AI and chip stocks tumbled last week, some investors sold gold to raise cash and meet margin calls. With Nvidia leading a sharp rebound in equities today, some of that selling pressure may be easing. Gold was already recovering before the US stock market opened, suggesting dip buyers were stepping in early. I’d characterize the move as a relief rally after last week’s liquidation, with the improvement in risk sentiment helping it along.

Technically, last week’s selloff took gold down to the upper edge of a swing area near $3,500. The price reached $3,502 on Friday before bouncing. Today’s low came in higher at $3,533.80, and the rebound has since taken gold back above $3,610.01, the 50% retracement of the move up from the 2022 low. The rally extended to $3,689.47 before pulling back.

For traders, $3,610.01 now defines the close risk. Stay above it and the buyers keep the short-term bias, with today’s high at $3,689.47 the first upside hurdle. Move back below it and the break loses traction, putting today’s low at $3,533.80 back in focus, followed by the $3,500 area that held on Friday.
In the video above, I take a more detailed look at where buyers stepped in, why the 50% retracement matters, and the levels that will tell us whether this rebound has more room to run.

news.title: U.S. Treasury sells $69 billion the two-year notes at a high yield of 4.700%
body: The auction stopped through the WI by 0.3 basis points, reversing the 0.3-basis-point tail at the prior auction. Bid to cover was just above average. The standout was direct demand, with bidders taking just over 6 percentage points more than usual. That more than made up for the shortfall in indirect participation and left dealers with a smaller share than average. The stop-through and lighter dealer takedown give the auction a B−.
